metadata.title: On the use of rational-function fitting methods for the solution of 2D Laplace boundary-value problems

extraction_notes.note: Numerical findings stated in prose around figures and a results table were emitted as claims with rigor numerical; the table and figures themselves are not nodes.
theorem or definition: one sentence both names the modified Dirichlet (Muskhelishvili) problem and asserts its unique solvability; typed by the solvability assertion.

The adaptive pole-addition procedure is one sentence carrying several operations; unmarked-algorithm steps would split a sentence, so it was left with zero steps.
Exterior Dirichlet and Neumann procedures are unmarked prose; the algorithm spans run from the method description to the end of the section and include explanatory sentences.

nodes.statement: \min_{P, Q} \left|\left|\dfrac{P - Q\widehat{W}}{\widehat{Q}}\right|\right|_\Gamma,

nodes.statement: \lambda(s) = \begin{cases} \lambda_1(s) & \text{if } h_0 \leq s < h_1\\ \lambda_2(s) & \text{if } h_1 \leq s < h_2\\ \vdots\\ \lambda_{M}(s) & \text{if } h_{M-1} \leq s < h_{M}\\ \end{cases},

nodes.statement: \lambda_m(s) = \dfrac{h_{m+1}-h_m}{\sqrt{(h_{m+1}-h_m)^2-\left(2s - h_{m+1}-h_m\right)^2}}.

nodes.statement: \rho(s_0) = \max\left(\left|s_0 + \sqrt{s_0^2-1}\right|, \left|s_0 - \sqrt{s_0^2-1}\right|\right).

nodes.statement: U|_{\mathrm{on} \ \Gamma_j} = f_j, \quad j = 1,2,\ldots J\\

nodes.statement: W(z) = \widetilde{W}(z) + \sum_{j=1}^{J}A_j \log\left(z-z^\Omega_j\right), \quad z^\Omega_j \in \Omega_j,

nodes.name: Constrained exterior Dirichlet least squares
nodes.statement: \begin{split} & \sum_{n = 0}^{N_\mathrm{out}} a_n^\mathrm{R} \phi_n^\mathrm{R}(z) - \sum_{n = 1}^{N_\mathrm{out}}a_n^\mathrm{I} \phi_n^\mathrm{I}(z) + \sum_{j=1}^{J}A_j \log\left|z-z^\Omega_j\right| \approx f(z), \\[1ex] & \text{with } f(z) = f_j(z) \quad \text{for } z \in \Gamma_j,\\ & \mathrm{subject \ to \ } \sum_{j=1}^{J}A_j = 0, \end{split}

nodes.name: Reduced exterior Dirichlet least squares
nodes.statement: \sum_{n = 0}^{N_\mathrm{out}} a_n^\mathrm{R} \phi_n^\mathrm{R}(z) - \sum_{n = 1}^{N_\mathrm{out}}a_n^\mathrm{I} \phi_n^\mathrm{I}(z) + \sum_{j=1}^{J-1}A_j \log\left|\dfrac{z-z^\Omega_j}{z-z^\Omega_{J}}\right| \approx f(z).

nodes.statement: \widetilde{W}(z) \approx f(z) - \sum_{j=1}^{J-1}A_j \log\left|\dfrac{z-z^\Omega_j}{z-z^\Omega_{J}}\right| + i\widehat{V}(z), \quad z \in \bigcup_{j=1}^{J}{\Gamma_j} = \Gamma.

nodes.name: Exterior Neumann problem
nodes.statement: \begin{split} & \nabla^2U(x,y) = 0, \quad \text{for all } (x,y) \notin \bigcup_{j=1}^{J}\Omega_j,\\ & {\left. \dfrac{\partial U}{\partial n} \right|_{{\text{on }}{\Gamma_j}}} = f_j,\\ & \lim_{|z|\rightarrow \infty}{\!\!U(x,y)|z|} < \infty, \quad z = x+iy, \end{split}

nodes.name: Neumann solvability condition
nodes.statement: \sum_{j=1}^{J}{\int_{\Gamma_j}{f_j(z)|dz|}} = 0.
nodes.label: eq:neumannCondition

nodes.name: Logarithmic coefficients A_j
nodes.statement: A_j = -\dfrac{1}{2 \pi}\int_{\Gamma_j}f_j(z)|dz|,
nodes.label: eq:logterm

nodes.name: Log-subtracted Neumann data
nodes.statement: \widetilde{f}_j(z) = f_j(z) - \sum_{j=1}^{J}A_j \log\left|z-z^J_j\right|,
nodes.label: eq:neumannSubtractLogs

nodes.name: Neumann condition for U-tilde
nodes.statement: \left.\dfrac{\partial \widetilde{U}}{\partial n}\right|_{\text{on }\Gamma_j} = \tilde{f}_j.
nodes.label: eq:tildeNeumann

nodes.name: Integrated condition for V-tilde
nodes.statement: \widetilde{V}(z) = \int_{z_j}^z{ \tilde{f}_j(z)|dz|} + v_j \equiv F_j(z) + v_j,

nodes.name: Neumann least-squares equations

nodes.name: Boundary estimate of W-tilde (Neumann)

nodes.name: Desingularized methods
nodes.statement: The technique described in this paper belongs to a class of methods known as desingularized methods, which are used for the solution of linear BVPs. What characterizes these methods is that the basis functions are elementary solutions of the homogenous PDE, and hence the singularities of the basis functions lie outside the BVP domain.
differentia: the basis functions are elementary solutions of the homogenous PDE
the singularities of the basis functions lie outside the BVP domain

nodes.name: Iteration not guaranteed to converge
nodes.statement: Clearly, the process just described is not guaranteed to converge to the solution that would be obtained were the imaginary part known in advance. It is possible that the estimated imaginary part will be inaccurate, and the poles found based on this estimate will not yield any improvement on the next iteration. When this happens, the improvement in accuracy stalls. It is then usually, though not always, possible to increase the accuracy further by increasing the number of poles. In numerical experiments, we have found that despite this difficulty, errors approaching the machine epsilon can be obtained for various challenging configurations.
nodes.statement_short: The pole/imaginary-part iteration may stall; adding poles usually helps, and machine-precision errors are observed in practice.

nodes.name: Dirichlet problem, simply-connected domain
nodes.statement: We begin by considering the simplest case, in which we seek a real valued potential, $U(x,y)$, which obeys the Laplace equation. More precisely, \begin{equation} \nabla^2U(x,y) =0, \quad \text{for all } (x,y) \in \Omega, \end{equation} where $\Omega$ is a simply connected domain in $\mathds{R}^2$ bounded by a curve $\Gamma$, and $U$ must also obey a Dirichlet boundary condition, \begin{equation} {\left. U \right|_{{\text{on }}{\Gamma}}} = f. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Find $U$ harmonic in a simply connected $\Omega$ with $U=f$ on its boundary $\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Complex potential W(z)
nodes.statement: As is well-known, the potential $U$ can be sought as the real part of a complex function $W(z)$, where $z= x + iy$ and $W(z)$ is holomorphic and single valued in $\Omega$ (it is single valued because $\Omega$ is simply connected).
nodes.statement_short: $U$ is the real part of a single-valued holomorphic complex potential $W(z)$, $z=x+iy$.

nodes.name: Single- and double-layer potentials
nodes.statement: The classical single- and double-layer potentials, \begin{equation} W_\text{single}(z) = \int_\Gamma \sigma(z')\log(z' - z)dz', \end{equation} and \begin{equation} W_\text{double}(z) = \dfrac{1}{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma \dfrac{\mu(z')}{z' - z}dz', \end{equation} where $\sigma(z)$ and $\mu(z)$ are referred to as the monopole and dipole densities, respectively, have been used extensively to formulate integral equations~\cite{mikhlin1957integral,atkinson1997numerical,greenbaum1993laplace}.
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited); Mikhlin 1957; Atkinson 1997; Greenbaum et al. 1993
nodes.statement_short: Classical single-layer (log kernel, monopole density) and double-layer (Cauchy kernel, dipole density) potentials.

nodes.name: Dipole-series representation of W
nodes.statement: Assuming that $W(z)$ is also holomorphic for $z \in \Gamma$, it can always be expressed as a series of complex dipole potentials, \begin{equation} W(z) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{a_n}{z'_n - z}, \quad \forall z \in \Omega, \end{equation} where the $z'_n$ are referred to as the poles of $W(z)$.
assumptions: Assuming that $W(z)$ is also holomorphic for $z \in \Gamma$
conclusions: it can always be expressed as a series of complex dipole potentials
nodes.statement_short: A $W$ holomorphic up to $\Gamma$ is a series of complex dipole potentials $a_n/(z'_n-z)$ with poles $z'_n$.

nodes.name: Wolff's theorem
nodes.statement: According to a theorem by Wolff~\cite{wolffRatFun} (see also~\cite[Ch.1, Theorem 13]{walsh1965interpolation}), given the appropriate choice of poles, $z'_n \notin \overline{\Omega}$,~\eqref{eq:ratFun} converges uniformly on any closed set in $\Omega$.
assumptions: given the appropriate choice of poles, $z'_n \notin \overline{\Omega}$
conclusions: ~\eqref{eq:ratFun} converges uniformly on any closed set in $\Omega$
nodes.statement_short: With suitable poles outside the closure of $\Omega$, the dipole series converges uniformly on closed subsets of $\Omega$.

nodes.name: N-pole rational approximation
nodes.statement: Our algorithm is based on approximating the complex potential using $N$ poles plus a constant, or equivalently as an $N^\text{th}$ order rational function \begin{equation} W(z) \approx a_0 + \sum_{n=1}^N \dfrac{a_n}{z'_n - z} = \dfrac{P_N(z)}{Q_N(z)} \end{equation} where $P_N$ and $Q_N$ are complex-coefficient polynomials of degree $N$.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate $W$ by a constant plus $N$ simple poles, i.e. a degree-$N$ rational function $P_N/Q_N$.

nodes.name: Dipole basis functions
nodes.statement: To determine $a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_N$, or equivalently, the coefficients of $P_N(z)$, we start with an initial guess for the poles, and associate a complex basis function with each pole, \begin{equation} \phi^\mathrm{C}_n(z) = \dfrac{1}{z'_n-z}, \end{equation} with real and imaginary parts, \begin{equation} \phi^\mathrm{R}_n(z) = \mathrm{Re}\left[\phi^\mathrm{C}_n(z)\right], \quad \phi^\mathrm{I}_n(z) = \mathrm{Im}\left[\phi^\mathrm{C}_n(z)\right]. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Complex basis function $1/(z'_n-z)$ per pole, with real and imaginary parts $\phi^R_n$, $\phi^I_n$.

nodes.name: Approximate potential and harmonic conjugate
nodes.statement: Defining $U(z) = \mathrm{Re}[W(z)]$ and $V(z) = \mathrm{Im}[W(z)]$, and using \eqref{eq:psiOfs}-\eqref{eq:constant}, \begin{align} U(z) & \approx \widehat{U}(z) = \sum_{n = 0}^{N} a_n^\mathrm{R} \phi_n^\mathrm{R}(z) - \sum_{n = 1}^{N}a_n^\mathrm{I} \phi_n^\mathrm{I}(z), \end{align} and its harmonic conjugate, \begin{align} V(z) & \approx \widehat{V}(z) = \sum_{n = 1}^{N} a_n^\mathrm{R} \phi_n^\mathrm{I}(z) + \sum_{n=1}^N a_n^\mathrm{I} \phi_n^\mathrm{R}(z), \end{align} where the basis function coefficients $a^\mathrm{R}_n \equiv \mathrm{Re}(a_n)$ and $a^\mathrm{I}_n \equiv \mathrm{Im}(a_n)$ are determined by minimizing an error metric on the boundary $\Gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: $\widehat U$ and its conjugate $\widehat V$ are real combinations of the dipole basis functions with coefficients $a_n^R, a_n^I$.

nodes.name: Residue least-squares problem
nodes.statement: More precisely, \begin{equation} \mathbf{a} \equiv [a_0^\mathrm{R}, a_1^\mathrm{R} + i a_1^\mathrm{I}, \ldots, a_N^\mathrm{R} + i a_N^\mathrm{I}]^T \end{equation} is determined by solving the minimization problem \begin{equation} \min_{\mathbf{a}} \left|\left|\widehat{U} - f\right|\right|_\Gamma \equiv \min_{\mathbf{a}} \left< \widehat{U}-f, \widehat{U}-f\right>_\Gamma^{\frac{1}{2}}, \end{equation} where the norm, $||\cdot||_\Gamma$, is induced by a Hermitian inner-product, $\left<\cdot, \cdot\right>_\Gamma$, the definition of which is deferred to Section~\ref{sec:innerProd}.
nodes.statement_short: Choose the residue vector $\mathbf a$ minimizing the boundary norm $\|\widehat U - f\|_\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Least squares equivalent to residual orthogonality
nodes.statement: The minimization in~\eqref{eq:minNormResidues} is equivalent to requiring that the residual, $f-\widehat{U}$, be orthogonal to the span of the basis functions, or equivalently, \begin{subequations} \begin{align} \left<\phi^{\mathrm{R}}_n, f - \widehat{U}\right>_\Gamma & = 0, \quad n = 0,1, \ldots, N,\\ \left<\phi^{\mathrm{I}}_n, f - \widehat{U}\right>_\Gamma & = 0, \quad n = 1, \ldots, N. \end{align} \end{subequations}
conclusions: The minimization in~\eqref{eq:minNormResidues} is equivalent to requiring that the residual, $f-\widehat{U}$, be orthogonal to the span of the basis functions
nodes.statement_short: Minimizing the norm is equivalent to Galerkin orthogonality of the residual to every basis function.

nodes.name: Pole relocation rational fitting problem
nodes.statement: The minimization problem is then \begin{equation} \min_{P, Q} \left|\left|\dfrac{P - Q\widehat{W}}{\widehat{Q}}\right|\right|_\Gamma, \end{equation} where $P$ and $Q$ are represented with polynomial bases, denoted $p_n$ and $q_n$, $n=0, 1, \ldots, N$, respectively. To avoid the trivial solution, $Q(z)$ is assumed to be monic in the $q_n$ basis.
nodes.statement_short: Linearized weighted rational fit $\min_{P,Q}\|(P-Q\widehat W)/\widehat Q\|_\Gamma$ with $Q$ monic.

nodes.name: Vector fitting (VF) basis
nodes.statement: In VF, the choice is $p_n(z) \equiv q_n(z) \equiv \ell_n(z)$, where \begin{equation} \ell_n(z) = \begin{cases} \widehat{Q}(z) & \mbox{if } n=0\\ \dfrac{\widehat{Q}(z)}{\left(z'_n-z\right)} & \mbox{if } 1 \le n \le N. \end{cases} \end{equation} For $n =1,2, \ldots, N$, the $\ell_n(z)$ are, up to a scaling factor, the Lagrange polynomials for interpolating at the $z'_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Vector fitting uses $p_n=q_n=\ell_n=\widehat Q/(z'_n-z)$ (scaled Lagrange polynomials at current poles).

nodes.name: Poles inside Omega are excluded
nodes.statement: When computing the roots of $Q(z)$ we may encounter roots inside $\Omega$. Although we do not discard these poles, their corresponding basis functions are not used to form $\widehat{U}(z)$ and $\widehat{V}(z)$. Hence, they are tacitly excluded from~\eqref{eq:approxU}-\eqref{eq:normalEquations}. As the algorithm progresses, these poles usually migrate outside of $\Omega$. Any poles that remain in $\Omega$ when the algorithm stops are discarded.
nodes.statement_short: Poles falling inside $\Omega$ are kept for relocation but excluded from the basis; those left at the end are discarded.

nodes.name: Initial pole guess heuristic
nodes.statement: The initial guess for the $z'_n$ is obtained by solving~\eqref{eq:Galerkin2} assuming $\widehat{W}(z) = f(z)$, which is purely real, $\widehat{Q}(z) = 1$, and then allowing $P$ and $Q$ to be of degree $2N$. Out of the $2N$ zeros of $Q$ we pick $N$ zeros that are outside $\Omega$, and, if there are not enough of these, we supplement them with zeros inside $\Omega$ so that we have $N$ zeros in total. These $N$ zeros are used as the poles for the first iteration.
output: These $N$ zeros are used as the poles for the first iteration.
nodes.statement_short: Fit a degree-$2N$ rational function to the real data $f$ and keep $N$ zeros of $Q$, preferring those outside $\Omega$.

nodes.name: Disk justification of the initial guess
nodes.statement: The justification for using $2N$ poles along with a purely real $\widehat{W}(z)$ is based on considering the fitting problem when $\Omega$ is a disk. For a disk, a purely real $\widehat{W}(z)$ can be constructed with $N$ poles inside $\Omega$ and $N$ poles outside $\Omega$. Using only the poles outside, we obtain a function that is holomorphic in the disk and its real part fits $f(z)$ on $\Gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: For a disk, a real $\widehat W$ uses $N$ poles inside and $N$ outside; the outside poles give a holomorphic fit of $f$.

nodes.name: Solve simply-connected Dirichlet problem (Algorithm 1)
nodes.statement: \caption{Solve simply-connected Dirichlet problem} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \STATE Set the $z'_n$ to the initial guess, as explained in Section~\ref{ssec:initial}. \WHILE {stopping criterion not met} \STATE Solve~\eqref{eq:normalEquations} for the $a^{\mathrm{R}}_n$ and $a^{\mathrm{I}}_n$. Use only $z'_n \notin \Omega$. \STATE Use the $a^{\mathrm{R}}_n$ and $a^{\mathrm{I}}_n$ to form $\widehat{V}$ according to~\eqref{eq:approxV} and $\widehat{W}$ according to~\eqref{eq:compPotToApprox}. \STATE Form $\widehat{Q}$ according to~\eqref{eq:QHat}, use all $z'_n$. \STATE Solve~\eqref{eq:Galerkin2} for $P$ and $Q$. \STATE $z'_n = \text{roots}(Q)$. \ENDWHILE \end{algorithmic}
input: Set the $z'_n$ to the initial guess
nodes.statement_short: Alternate solving for residues by least squares and relocating poles as roots of a rational fit to $f+i\widehat V$.
nodes.label: alg:main

nodes.name: Generic boundary norm-minimization problem
nodes.statement: Both problems can be formulated as follows: given a set basis functions $\psi_1, \psi_2, \ldots \psi_{N_\psi}$ defined on $\Gamma$, and a function to approximate, $g$, also defined on $\Gamma$, we wish to determine the vector of coefficients $\mathbf{c}$ that solves the norm minimization problem \begin{equation} \min_{\mathbf{c}} \left\|\sum_{n=1}^{N_\psi} c_n\psi_n - g\right\|_\Gamma. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3 Inner product definition and quadrature rules
nodes.statement_short: Find coefficients $\mathbf c$ minimizing $\|\sum c_n\psi_n - g\|_\Gamma$ for given basis functions and target $g$.

nodes.name: Gram-matrix solution of least squares
nodes.statement: The unique solution to this problem is given by \begin{equation} \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{\Psi}^{-1}\mathbf{g_\psi}, \end{equation} where $\mathbf{\Psi}_{mn} = \left<\psi_m,\psi_n\right>_\Gamma$ and $(\mathbf{g_\psi})_m = \left<g,\psi_m\right>_\Gamma$.
nodes.section: 3 Inner product definition and quadrature rules
conclusions: The unique solution to this problem is given by
nodes.statement_short: The minimizer is $\mathbf c = \Psi^{-1}\mathbf g_\psi$ with Gram matrix $\Psi$.

nodes.name: Gram matrix is Hermitian positive definite
nodes.statement: It can be easily shown that $\mathbf{\Psi}$ is Hermitian positive definite and hence invertible, provided that the $\psi_n$ are linearly independent (that this is so for the $\phi_n^\mathrm{R}$ and $\phi_n^\mathrm{I}$ follows from a trivial modification of Theorem 4 in~\cite{kupradze1967approximate}, where it was proved in a 3D context).
nodes.section: 3 Inner product definition and quadrature rules
assumptions: provided that the $\psi_n$ are linearly independent
conclusions: $\mathbf{\Psi}$ is Hermitian positive definite and hence invertible
nodes.statement_short: $\Psi$ is HPD (hence invertible) when the basis is linearly independent, which holds for the dipole basis by Kupradze's Theorem 4.

nodes.name: Weighted boundary inner product
nodes.statement: The inner product used in this work is \begin{equation} \left<u,v\right>_\Gamma = \int_0^1 u\left(z(s)\right)v^*\left(z(s)\right)\lambda(s)ds, \end{equation} where $\lambda(s)$ denotes a positive weight function, and $z(s)$ is a parametrization of $\Gamma$.
nodes.section: 3 Inner product definition and quadrature rules

nodes.name: Exact quadrature recovers the continuous least-squares solution
nodes.statement: If the quadrature rule is exact, then the solution given in~\eqref{eq:LSAnalytic} also solves~\eqref{eq:continuousLS} (see, e.g.,~\cite[Ch. 4]{atkinson1997numerical}).
nodes.section: 3 Inner product definition and quadrature rules
assumptions: If the quadrature rule is exact
conclusions: the solution given in~\eqref{eq:LSAnalytic} also solves~\eqref{eq:continuousLS}

nodes.name: Piecewise rational boundary parametrization
nodes.statement: However, the parametrization of $z(s)$ is ours to choose, and we choose it to be a piecewise rational function, i.e., \begin{equation} z(s) = \begin{cases} r_1(s) & \text{if } 0 \leq s < h_1\\ r_2(s) & \text{if } h_1 \leq s < h_2\\ \vdots\\ r_{M}(s) & \text{if } h_{M-1} \leq s < 1\\ \end{cases}, \end{equation} where the $r_m(s)$ are rational functions in $s$.

nodes.name: Exactness of rational Gauss-Chebyshev quadrature
nodes.statement: These rules integrate exactly integrals of the form \begin{equation} \int_{-1}^{1}{R(s)T^*(s^*)}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-s^2}}ds, \end{equation} where $R(s)$ and $T(s)$ are rational functions that have poles at known locations (and need not be proper)~\cite{van2008algorithm}.
assumptions: $R(s)$ and $T(s)$ are rational functions that have poles at known locations (and need not be proper)
conclusions: These rules integrate exactly integrals of the form
nodes.statement_short: Rational Gauss-Chebyshev rules integrate $\int R(s)T^*(s^*)/\sqrt{1-s^2}$ exactly for rationals with known poles.

nodes.name: Chebyshev-type inner-product weight
nodes.statement: Using these quadrature rules implies a specific choice for the inner-product weight function, denoted $\lambda(s)$ in~\eqref{eq:ip}, namely, \begin{equation} \lambda(s) = \begin{cases} \lambda_1(s) & \text{if } h_0 \leq s < h_1\\ \lambda_2(s) & \text{if } h_1 \leq s < h_2\\ \vdots\\ \lambda_{M}(s) & \text{if } h_{M-1} \leq s < h_{M}\\ \end{cases}, \end{equation} where \begin{equation} \lambda_m(s) = \dfrac{h_{m+1}-h_m}{\sqrt{(h_{m+1}-h_m)^2-\left(2s - h_{m+1}-h_m\right)^2}}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The weight is a Chebyshev weight scaled to each parameter interval $[h_m,h_{m+1})$.

nodes.name: Poles at infinity raise polynomial exactness
nodes.statement: Adding $N_\infty$ poles at infinity makes the quadrature rule exact for integrands that are products of a rational function and a polynomial of degree $2N_\infty-1$.
conclusions: makes the quadrature rule exact for integrands that are products of a rational function and a polynomial of degree $2N_\infty-1$

nodes.name: Chebyshev interpolation error on Bernstein ellipses
nodes.statement: The max-norm error of the polynomial that interpolates at Chebyshev nodes is almost minimal and it is the same for all $s_0$ on the ellipse \begin{equation} s(\phi) = \dfrac{\rho e^{i\phi} + \rho^{-1} e^{-i\phi}}{2}, \quad \phi \in [0, 2 \pi], \end{equation} where $\rho>1$ is the so-called \emph{elliptical radius} (see, e.g.,~\cite{trefethen2009approximation}).
conclusions: The max-norm error of the polynomial that interpolates at Chebyshev nodes is almost minimal and it is the same for all $s_0$ on the ellipse
nodes.statement_short: Chebyshev interpolation of a pole function is near-minimax, with error depending only on the elliptical radius $\rho$ of the pole.

nodes.name: Froissart doublets
nodes.statement: The reason is related to the occurrence of pole-zero pairs, called Froissart doublets~\cite{froissart1969approximation,gilewicz1999pade,pach�n2009piecewise}, which almost coincide with the boundary. These pole-zero pairs are a numerical artifact, and they do not contribute to the fidelity of the fit, but instead they fit errors in the data.
nodes.origin_citation: Froissart 1969; Gilewicz & Kryakin; Pachon et al.

nodes.name: Quadrature scheme tolerates near-boundary poles
nodes.statement: By using the proposed quadrature scheme, all the poles outside of $\Omega$, no matter how close they are to its boundary, can be safely used to solve~\eqref{eq:minNormResidues}.
conclusions: all the poles outside of $\Omega$, no matter how close they are to its boundary, can be safely used to solve~\eqref{eq:minNormResidues}

nodes.name: Exterior Dirichlet problem
nodes.statement: In the exterior Dirichlet problem, the potential $U(x,y)$ obeys the Laplace equation everywhere outside of a set of disjoint domains $\Omega_1, \Omega_2, \ldots, \Omega_J$ bounded by contours $\Gamma_1, \Gamma_2, \ldots, \Gamma_J$, respectively. As before, Dirichlet boundary conditions are imposed, \begin{equation} U|_{\mathrm{on} \ \Gamma_j} = f_j, \quad j = 1,2,\ldots J\\ \end{equation} and in addition, the potential must be bounded at infinity.
nodes.statement_short: Find $U$ harmonic outside disjoint domains $\Omega_j$, equal to $f_j$ on $\Gamma_j$ and bounded at infinity.

nodes.name: Logarithmic decomposition of the exterior complex potential
nodes.statement: Also, the complex potential $W(z)$ is no longer single-valued, but can be written as the sum of $J$ logarithmic terms and a single-valued holomorphic function $\widetilde{W}(z)$ (see, e.g.,~\cite[\S{29}]{mikhlin1957integral}). We have, \begin{equation} W(z) = \widetilde{W}(z) + \sum_{j=1}^{J}A_j \log\left(z-z^\Omega_j\right), \quad z^\Omega_j \in \Omega_j, \end{equation} where the $A_j$ may be assumed real, and the $z^\Omega_j$ can be anywhere inside $\Omega_j$, preferably as far from its boundary as possible.
conclusions: can be written as the sum of $J$ logarithmic terms and a single-valued holomorphic function $\widetilde{W}(z)$
nodes.statement_short: In the exterior domain $W$ = single-valued holomorphic $\widetilde W$ plus $J$ real-coefficient logarithms centered in the $\Omega_j$.

nodes.name: Exterior Dirichlet iteration
nodes.statement: If the $A_j$ were known, the logarithmic terms could be subtracted from the boundary data, and the algorithm for the simply-connected Dirichlet problem could be applied to $\widetilde{W}(z)$. Our approach is therefore to estimate the $A_j$ iteratively, along with the imaginary part of $\widetilde{W}(z)$. On each iteration, we solve \begin{equation} \begin{split} & \sum_{n = 0}^{N_\mathrm{out}} a_n^\mathrm{R} \phi_n^\mathrm{R}(z) - \sum_{n = 1}^{N_\mathrm{out}}a_n^\mathrm{I} \phi_n^\mathrm{I}(z) + \sum_{j=1}^{J}A_j \log\left|z-z^\Omega_j\right| \approx f(z), \\[1ex] & \text{with } f(z) = f_j(z) \quad \text{for } z \in \Gamma_j,\\ & \mathrm{subject \ to \ } \sum_{j=1}^{J}A_j = 0, \end{split} \end{equation} for the $a_n^\mathrm{R}$, the $a_n^\mathrm{I}$, and the $A_j$. The condition that the sum of $A_j$'s is zero, needed to ensure the solution is bounded at infinity, can be enforced by eliminating one of the $A_j$, say, $A_{J} = - \sum_{j=1}^{J-1}A_j$. Instead of~\eqref{eq:exteriorDirichlet} we then have, \begin{equation} \sum_{n = 0}^{N_\mathrm{out}} a_n^\mathrm{R} \phi_n^\mathrm{R}(z) - \sum_{n = 1}^{N_\mathrm{out}}a_n^\mathrm{I} \phi_n^\mathrm{I}(z) + \sum_{j=1}^{J-1}A_j \log\left|\dfrac{z-z^\Omega_j}{z-z^\Omega_{J}}\right| \approx f(z). \end{equation} As before, we solve~\eqref{eq:exteriorDirichlet2} by sampling at quadrature nodes, weighting the equation by the square roots of the quadrature weights, and solving the linear system in the least-squares sense. In contrast to the previous case, however, the inner products involving the logarithmic basis functions will not be integrated exactly. We must therefore add poles at infinity when deriving the quadrature rules for each section of the boundary. Fortunately, the logarithmic singularity is weak, so when the $z^\Omega_j$ are not too close to the boundary, the restriction of the logarithmic term to the boundary curve can be approximated well by piecewise polynomials. The poles at infinity added by the pole-pruning process of Section~\ref{sec:pruning} usually suffice, although extra poles at infinity can be added if necessary. Once~\eqref{eq:exteriorDirichlet2} has been solved, a rational function is fitted to an estimate of the boundary values of $\widetilde{W}(z)$, \begin{equation} \widetilde{W}(z) \approx f(z) - \sum_{j=1}^{J-1}A_j \log\left|\dfrac{z-z^\Omega_j}{z-z^\Omega_{J}}\right| + i\widehat{V}(z), \quad z \in \bigcup_{j=1}^{J}{\Gamma_j} = \Gamma. \end{equation} The real part is estimated as $f(z)$, the known values of $\mathrm{Re}[W(z)]$ on the boundaries, with the real part of the logarithmic terms subtracted. The estimate for $\mathrm{Im}[\widetilde{W}(z)]$ is $\widehat{V}(z)$, given by~\eqref{eq:approxV}, and it remains as it was for the simply-connected problem when $\widetilde{W}(z)$ and $W(z)$ were the same.
output: a rational function is fitted to an estimate of the boundary values of $\widetilde{W}(z)$
nodes.statement_short: Estimate log coefficients $A_j$ jointly with residues by constrained least squares, then fit poles to the log-subtracted $\widetilde W$.

nodes.name: Exterior Neumann problem
nodes.statement: For brevity, we discuss only the exterior problem, which can be formulated as \begin{equation} \begin{split} & \nabla^2U(x,y) = 0, \quad \text{for all } (x,y) \notin \bigcup_{j=1}^{J}\Omega_j,\\ & {\left. \dfrac{\partial U}{\partial n} \right|_{{\text{on }}{\Gamma_j}}} = f_j,\\ & \lim_{|z|\rightarrow \infty}{\!\!U(x,y)|z|} < \infty, \quad z = x+iy, \end{split} \end{equation} where the $\Omega_j$ are again simple disjoint domains bounded by the $\Gamma_j$.
nodes.statement_short: Find $U$ harmonic outside the $\Omega_j$ with prescribed normal derivative $f_j$ and decay at infinity.

nodes.name: Solvability condition for the exterior Neumann problem
nodes.statement: This problem is uniquely solvable if and only if \begin{equation} \sum_{j=1}^{J}{\int_{\Gamma_j}{f_j(z)|dz|}} = 0. \end{equation}
conclusions: This problem is uniquely solvable if and only if
nodes.statement_short: The exterior Neumann problem is uniquely solvable iff the total boundary flux vanishes.

nodes.name: Exterior Neumann iteration
nodes.statement: The approach we adopt for this problem follows~\cite[\S{32}]{mikhlin1957integral}. As in the exterior Dirichlet problem, we seek the solution as the real part of a function $W(z)$ that is holomorphic outside the $\Omega_j$, and which can be written as a sum of a single-valued part, $\widetilde{W}(z)$, and $J$ logarithmic terms. In this case, however, the logarithmic terms are known in advance: \begin{equation} A_j = -\dfrac{1}{2 \pi}\int_{\Gamma_j}f_j(z)|dz|, \end{equation} and they can be subtracted from the boundary data. After this subtraction, \begin{equation} \widetilde{f}_j(z) = f_j(z) - \sum_{j=1}^{J}A_j \log\left|z-z^J_j\right|, \end{equation} can be used to write a Neumann boundary condition for $\mathrm{Re}\left[\widetilde{W}(z)\right]$. Denoting $\widetilde{W}(z) = \widetilde{U}(z) + i \widetilde{V}(z)$, this condition reads, \begin{equation} \left.\dfrac{\partial \widetilde{U}}{\partial n}\right|_{\text{on }\Gamma_j} = \tilde{f}_j. \end{equation} If $\widetilde{W}(z)$ is approximated by a weighted combination of dipole potentials, it becomes inconvenient to enforce~\eqref{eq:tildeNeumann} directly, as the differentiation increases the order of the poles. Instead, we integrate~\eqref{eq:tildeNeumann} with respect to arc-length and use the Cauchy-Riemann equations to obtain, \begin{equation} \widetilde{V}(z) = \int_{z_j}^z{ \tilde{f}_j(z)|dz|} + v_j \equiv F_j(z) + v_j, \end{equation} where the integration is along $\Gamma_j$, from an arbitrary point $z_j$ to the point $z$, and the $v_j$ are constants yet to be determined. Finding a harmonic function $\widetilde{V}$ that satisfies the boundary condition~\eqref{eq:vtilde} is known as a modified Dirichlet~\cite{mikhlin1957integral} or Muskhelishvili~\cite{pogorzelski1966integral} problem, and given the condition at infinity in~\eqref{eq:neumann}, it is solvable only for a unique set of $v_j$ constants. These can be determined along with an approximate solution for $\widetilde{V}$, by solving \begin{equation} \sum_{n = 1}^{N_\mathrm{out}} a_n^\mathrm{R} \phi_n^\mathrm{I}(z) + a_n^\mathrm{I} \phi_n^\mathrm{R}(z) - v_j \approx F_j(z), \quad \text{for} \ z \in \Gamma_j, \end{equation} for the $a^\mathrm{R}_n$, the $a^\mathrm{I}_n$, and the $v_j$. As before,~\eqref{eq:neumannResidues} is solved in the least-squares sense after sampling the basis functions at quadrature nodes and weighting the equations by the square roots of quadrature weights. Once~\eqref{eq:neumannResidues} is solved, the rational fitting algorithm is applied to an estimate of the boundary values of $\widetilde{W}(z)$ given by, \begin{equation} \widetilde{W}(z) \approx \sum_{n = 1}^{N_\mathrm{out}} a_n^\mathrm{I} \phi_n^\mathrm{I}(z) + a_n^\mathrm{R} \phi_n^\mathrm{R}(z) + i \left[ F_j(z) + v_j\right], \quad \text{for} \ z \in \Gamma_j. \end{equation} As expected, in the Neumann problem, it is the \emph{imaginary} part of the complex potential that is prescribed by the boundary data (up to $J$ additive constants), while its real part and the $J$ constants are estimated iteratively. Note that the $n=0$ term corresponding to the constant basis function is omitted from the sum in~\eqref{eq:whNeumann} so as to conform with the boundary condition at infinity in~\eqref{eq:neumann}.
input: the normal derivative of the potential on the boundary
output: the rational fitting algorithm is applied to an estimate of the boundary values of $\widetilde{W}(z)$
nodes.statement_short: Subtract known log terms, integrate the Neumann data to a modified Dirichlet condition on $\widetilde V$, and iterate residue fitting and pole relocation.

nodes.name: Unique solvability of the modified Dirichlet (Muskhelishvili) problem
nodes.statement: Finding a harmonic function $\widetilde{V}$ that satisfies the boundary condition~\eqref{eq:vtilde} is known as a modified Dirichlet~\cite{mikhlin1957integral} or Muskhelishvili~\cite{pogorzelski1966integral} problem, and given the condition at infinity in~\eqref{eq:neumann}, it is solvable only for a unique set of $v_j$ constants.
assumptions: given the condition at infinity in~\eqref{eq:neumann}
conclusions: it is solvable only for a unique set of $v_j$ constants

nodes.name: Advantages of the dipole Neumann formulation
nodes.statement: The formulation just described differs from one that is commonly used for Neumann problems in integral-equation formulations (e.g., in~\cite{greenbaum1993laplace}). These formulations typically use a single-layer potential so that enforcing the boundary condition of~\eqref{eq:neumann} leads to a second-kind Fredholm equation. We could have formulated our solution similarly, i.e., by representing the potential as a weighted combination of monopole potentials. Enforcing the boundary condition would then lead to a weighted combination of dipole potentials approximating the normal derivative of $U$. The chosen formulation does have some advantages, however. First, the functions to be approximated, the $F_j(s)$, are smoother than the $f_j(s)$, so fewer basis functions may be needed for their approximation. Second, a common situation in Neumann problems is that the $A_j$ of~\eqref{eq:logterm} are zero, so that the complex potential $W(z)$ is single valued. This occurs when the boundary is composed of a single contour, or when the $\Omega_j$ represent impenetrable objects. In these cases, it is convenient to approximate $W(z)$ using single-valued basis functions, instead of having a superposition of non-single-valued functions that can be made single-valued by an appropriate choice of branch cuts, as would occur if monopoles were used. For instance, using the proposed formulation, it is easy to obtain equipotential contours and field lines as the level sets of $\mathrm{Re}\left[W(z)\right]$ and $\mathrm{Im}\left[W(z)\right]$, without having to keep track of the proper Riemann-sheet on which to evaluate the logarithmic kernel.
nodes.statement_short: Approximating integrated data with dipoles gives smoother targets and single-valued potentials, unlike monopole/single-layer formulations.

nodes.name: Cluster partitioning scheme for large-scale problems
nodes.statement: We propose a scheme for geometries made up of a large number of simple closed curves. The scheme consists of partitioning the boundary curves into clusters so that each curve belongs to a single cluster, as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:clust}. \begin{figure}[h] \centering \rotatebox{270}{\scalebox{0.4}{\includegraphics{clust.eps}}} \caption{Boundary curves partitioned into three clusters with buffer regions (delimited by dashed lines).} \end{figure} Various algorithms for obtaining such a partition exist, and we use the simplest one, the $k$-means clustering, or Lloyd's, algorithm~\cite{lloyd1982least}. To keep the partitioning simple, each curve is entirely within one cluster and represented by its centroid, on which the clustering algorithm operates. Then, to each cluster we add a ``buffer region,'' as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:clust}, so that curves close to the edge of the cluster have all their nearby interactions taken into account. The buffer region is obtained by adding to each curve all the curves with centroids closer than some radius, and this radius is chosen as twice the distance to the nearest centroid among all other curves. Poles that, after the local optimization, are found inside the buffer region are not used when solving the full problem.
input: geometries made up of a large number of simple closed curves
nodes.statement_short: Cluster curves by $k$-means on centroids, add buffer regions, optimize poles per cluster, and drop buffer poles for the global solve.

nodes.name: Normalized error Delta E
nodes.statement: The error metric adopted in this work is $\Delta E$, \begin{equation} \Delta E = \dfrac{\|\mathbf{\hat{u}} - \mathbf{f}\|_w}{\|\mathbf{f}\|_w}, \end{equation} where $\mathbf{f}$ and $\mathbf{\hat{u}}$ are vectors of samples at the quadrature points of the exact and approximate boundary values, respectively. The $\|\cdot\|_w$ norm includes multiplication by the quadrature weights, so that it is an approximation of the continuous norm.

nodes.name: Residual is largest on the boundary
nodes.statement: The residual, $\widehat{U} -U$, is itself a harmonic function throughout $\overline{\Omega}$ and hence is largest at the boundary.
assumptions: The residual, $\widehat{U} -U$, is itself a harmonic function throughout $\overline{\Omega}$
conclusions: is largest at the boundary

nodes.name: Maximum-norm error Delta E_max
nodes.statement: We also used the maximum-norm error, \begin{equation} \Delta E_\mathrm{max} = \dfrac{\underset{z \in \Gamma}{\max}\left|f(z) - \widehat{U}(z)\right|}{{||f(z)||_{L^2(\Gamma)}/||1||_{L^2(\Gamma)}}}, \end{equation} where $||1||_{L^2(\Gamma)}$ is just the length of $\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Ellipse with six-pole boundary data
nodes.statement: A plot of error vs. iteration count is shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:ellipse}, for an ellipse with unit semi-major axis and an aspect ratio of two, and boundary data as in~\eqref{eq:simpleF} with $N_0 = 6, a^0_k = k/N_0$, and $z'_k = 1.5\exp\left[i\pi (2k+1)/6\right]$.

nodes.name: One extra pole restores exponential convergence
nodes.statement: When $N=N_0$, the error does not decrease much below 0.1\%, but when $N=N_0+1$, the error drops exponentially, approaching the machine epsilon after 45 iterations.
conclusions: the error drops exponentially, approaching the machine epsilon after 45 iterations

nodes.name: Adaptive pole addition
nodes.statement: For example, one can calculate $\sigma_K(\Delta E)$, the standard deviation of $\Delta E$ in the previous $K$ iterations, and add a pole whenever \begin{equation} \sigma_K(\Delta E) < \mu_K(\Delta E) \epsilon, \end{equation} where $\mu_K(\Delta E)$ is the $K$-average of $\Delta E$ and $\epsilon$ is a small number.
nodes.statement_short: Add a pole whenever the relative standard deviation of $\Delta E$ over the last $K$ iterations drops below $\epsilon$.

nodes.name: Trigonometric boundary curves with ten-pole data
nodes.statement:
We consider next boundary curves of the form,  egin{equation} z(s) = \left[1/\gamma + (1/\gamma-1)\cos(2 \pi 
u s)ight] e^{j2 \pi s},\quad s \in [0,1] \end{equation} with $\gamma = 1.75$, and $
u = 2,4,6.$ A plot of the $
u = 6$ curve is shown in Fig.~ef{fig:trigpolyGeom}, together with a set of ten points distributed on a circle of radius $R$, which represent the poles of the boundary data.

nodes.name: Method works best when data poles are near the boundary
nodes.statement: We see that, in contrast to conventional desingularized- and integral-equation- methods, the proposed method works best when the poles of $f$ are close to the boundary, adding only a few spurious poles during the solution.
conclusions: the proposed method works best when the poles of $f$ are close to the boundary, adding only a few spurious poles during the solution

nodes.name: Almost-singular boundary data on an ellipse
nodes.statement: In the next example, the boundary is an ellipse with unit semi-minor axis, and an aspect ratio of two, and the boundary data is, \begin{equation} f(z) = \mathrm{Re}\left\{\exp\left[\dfrac{1}{z-1.01}\right]\right\}, \quad z\ \in \Gamma. \end{equation} This implies that the exact complex potential has an essential singularity very close to the boundary.

nodes.name: Accuracy for almost-singular data
nodes.statement: Nevertheless, errors on the order of $\Delta E_\mathrm{max} = 10^{-11}$ are obtained with no more than 25 poles (Fig.~\ref{fig:essential}).
conclusions: errors on the order of $\Delta E_\mathrm{max} = 10^{-11}$ are obtained with no more than 25 poles

nodes.name: Green's-function problem with almost-sharp tips
nodes.statement: In the next example, we consider a Green's-function type problem, where a boundary curve of form~\eqref{eq:trigpoly} with $\nu = 2$ is excited by a monopole potential, \begin{equation} f(s) = \log|z(s)|. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Approximately exponential convergence in the number of poles
nodes.statement: The rate of convergence with respect to the number of poles is approximately exponential, and the minimal error obtained is similar to that of the Nystr\"{o}m method.
conclusions: The rate of convergence with respect to the number of poles is approximately exponential

nodes.name: Exponential clustering of poles at a reentrant corner
nodes.statement: The distances, which are normalized with respect to the distance of the exciting line-source from the corner, are seen to decrease at an almost constant exponential rate, with the closest poles clustered even more densely.
conclusions: are seen to decrease at an almost constant exponential rate

nodes.name: Condition number grows while residue norm decreases
nodes.statement: As shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:cornerConv}b, the condition number increases with $N$, but the norm of the vector of residues (normalized with respect to $N$) decreases.
conclusions: the condition number increases with $N$, but the norm of the vector of residues (normalized with respect to $N$) decreases

nodes.name: Two nearly touching circles (exterior Dirichlet)
nodes.statement: An example of this sort consists of two circular curves with boundary values $-1$ on the lower curve and $+1$ on the upper one, and relative separations $d/R = 0.01, 0.1, 0.5$, as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:twoCylinders}.

nodes.name: Logarithmic scaling with separation
nodes.statement: To a good approximation, the $N$ needed to achieve a given error scales like $1/d$ when using the Nystr\"{o}m method, but it scales like $\log(1/d)$ when using the proposed method.
conclusions: it scales like $\log(1/d)$ when using the proposed method
nodes.statement_short: Required $N$ grows like $1/d$ for Nystrom but only like $\log(1/d)$ for the proposed method as curves approach.

nodes.name: Potential flow around many random ellipses
nodes.statement: In the last example, we solve a Neumann problem of potential flow around impenetrable ellipses of random radius, eccentricity, and orientation, many of which are very close to one another. This geometry was generated by a simple modification of the method described in~\cite{helsing2008evaluation} for generating a distribution of random circles. The velocity field far from the ellipses is assumed uniform, of unit amplitude, and in the $x$ direction. The corresponding BVP is then given by~\eqref{eq:neumann} with $f_j(z) = -\cos\left[\theta_j(z)\right]$ where $\theta_j(z)$ is the angle between the outward-pointing normal to the $j^\text{th}$ curve and the $x$ axis.

nodes.name: Equal convex hulls of Helmholtz and Laplace singularities
nodes.statement: For exterior problems, it was shown in~\cite{millar1980analytic} that the convex hull of singularities of Helmholtz and Laplace BVPs are the same, assuming the same boundary data.
conclusions: the convex hull of singularities of Helmholtz and Laplace BVPs are the same

nodes.name: Laplace pole hull guides Helmholtz source placement
nodes.statement: In particular, locating the Helmholtz sources so that they enclose the convex hull of singularities of the Laplace problem guarantees that all of the singularities of the Helmholtz problem are enclosed. According to the conjectures in~\cite{barnett2008stability}, which have recently been proved~\cite{kangro2010convergence}, this guarantees exponential convergence.
assumptions: locating the Helmholtz sources so that they enclose the convex hull of singularities of the Laplace problem
conclusions: guarantees that all of the singularities of the Helmholtz problem are enclosed
this guarantees exponential convergence

nodes.name: Iterated rational fitting (IRF) with Arnoldi orthonormalization
nodes.statement:
The IRF method we use is based on a variant of~\cite{coelho1999robust} presented in~\cite{vasilyevequivalence}. As explained in Section~ef{sec:poleReloc}, we seek a rational function $P/Q$ that approximates $\widehat{W}$, and we do so by solving weighted linear least-squares problems of the from~\eqref{eq:minProbIRF}. Using the quadrature rules of Section~ef{ssec:quadForIRF}, we discretize the continuous norm in~\eqref{eq:minProbIRF} and write the minimization problem as,  egin{equation} \min_{\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}} \, \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{n=0}^N{ \dfrac{\sqrt{\lambda_k}}{\widehat{Q}(z_k)}\left|{b_n z_k^n - a_n z_k^n \widehat{W}(z_k) }ight|} \end{equation} in which the unknowns are the monomial coefficients of $P(z)$ and $Q(z)$, denoted $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{a}$, respectively. To avoid the trivial solution, a normalization condition, to be specified below, must be imposed on one of the polynomials. Let us rewrite~\eqref{eq:minProb} in matrix form, using the notation  egin{align} \mathbf{\Lambda} &= 	ext{diag}(\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots, \lambda_K),
otag \ \mathbf{\widehat{Q}} &= 	ext{diag}\left[\widehat{Q}(z_1), \widehat{Q}(z_2), \ldots, \widehat{Q}(z_K)ight],
otag \ \mathbf{\widehat{W}} &= 	ext{diag}\left[\widehat{W}(z_1), \widehat{W}(z_2), \ldots, \widehat{W}(z_K)ight],\ V_{kn} &= z_k^n, \quad n=0,1,\ldots,N,
otag \ \mathbf{c} &=  egin{bmatrix} \mathbf{b}\ \mathbf{a}\ \end{bmatrix}.
otag \end{align} We obtain,  egin{equation} \min_{\mathbf{c}} \, \left|\left|\mathbf{\Lambda}^ rac{1}{2} \mathbf{\widehat{Q}}^{-1}\left[\mathbf{V}, -\mathbf{\widehat{W}}\mathbf{V}ight]\mathbf{c}ight|ight|. \end{equation} The conditioning of the Vandermonde matrix, $\mathbf{V}$, can be very poor (sampling points on the real line, for example), or very good (sampling points on the unit circle, for example), and this can affect the conditioning of the minimization problem~\eqref{eq:irfDiscrete}. To deal with this problem, we construct two orthonormal bases, one for the column space of $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{\Lambda}^ rac{1}{2} \mathbf{\widehat{Q}}^{-1}\mathbf{V}$ and one for the column space of $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{\Lambda}^ rac{1}{2} \mathbf{\widehat{Q}}^{-1}\mathbf{\widehat{W}V}$. This can be done with the Arnoldi iteration~\cite{arnoldi1951principle,saad2003iterative}, by noting that the columns of $\mathbf{A}$ form a Krylov subspace,  egin{equation} K= 	ext{span}[\mathbf{d}, \mathbf{Z}\mathbf{d}, \mathbf{Z}^2\mathbf{d}, \ldots, \mathbf{Z}^N\mathbf{d}], \end{equation} where $\mathbf{Z} = \mathrm{diag}\left(z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_Kight)$ and $\mathbf{d} = \mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{\Lambda}^ rac{1}{2} \mathbf{\widehat{Q}}^{-1})$, and similarly for the columns of $\mathbf{B}$. Once we have constructed the orthonormal bases,  egin{align} \mathrm{colsp}(\mathbf{P}) &= \mathrm{colsp}(\mathbf{A}), \quad \mathbf{P^\dagger P} = \mathbf{I} \ \mathrm{colsp}(\mathbf{Q}) &= \mathrm{colsp}(\mathbf{B}), \quad \mathbf{Q^\dagger Q} = \mathbf{I}, \end{align} we rewrite~\eqref{eq:irfDiscrete} in the new basis,  egin{equation} \min_{\mathbf{	ilde{c}}} \, \left|\left|\left[\mathbf{P}, -\mathbf{Q}ight]\mathbf{	ilde{c}}ight|ight|, \end{equation} and impose the normalization condition $	ilde{c}_{2N} = 1$, which corresponds to $Q(z)$ being monic in the new basis. The solution of the minimization problem is then obtained by solving the over-determined linear system  egin{equation} [\mathbf{P},-\mathbf{Q}_{1:N-1}]\mathbf{	ilde{c}} = \mathbf{Q}_N \end{equation} in the least-squares sense. In~\eqref{eq:irfLS}, we denote the column corresponding to the $N$th-degree polynomial basis function by $\mathbf{Q}_{N}$, while the rest of the $\mathbf{Q}$ matrix is denoted by $\mathbf{Q}_{1:N-1}$. The numerical stability of~\eqref{eq:irfDiscretePQ} is generally much better than that of~\eqref{eq:irfDiscrete}, as the unknowns are coefficients of two sets of orthonormal columns. Once~\eqref{eq:irfDiscrete} is solved, the zeros of $Q(z)$, which are the poles for the next iteration, can be obtained without transforming back to the monomial basis. They are the eigenvalues of a generalized companion matrix~\cite{coelho1999robust},  egin{equation} \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{H}_{1:N,1:N} - H_{N+1,N}\,\mathbf{	ilde{c}}_{N+1:2N}\,\mathbf{e}_N^T, \end{equation} where $\mathbf{e}_N$ is the $N^	ext{th}$ column of the order-$N$ identity matrix and $\mathbf{H}$ is the upper Hessenberg matrix obtained from the Arnoldi iteration used to generate the orthonormal basis for colsp($\mathbf{B}$).
output: the zeros of $Q(z)$, which are the poles for the next iteration
nodes.statement_short: Linearized rational least squares with Arnoldi-orthonormalized bases for $P$ and $Q$; new poles from a generalized companion matrix.

nodes.name: Winding-integral test for poles inside D
nodes.statement: Using Cauchy's theorem, a pole $z'$ is inside $D$ if and only if \begin{equation} \int_C \dfrac{1}{z-z'}dz = \int_0^1 \dfrac{1}{z(s)-z'}\dfrac{dz(s)}{ds} \,ds = 2\pi i \end{equation}
nodes.section: B Determining whether a pole is inside $D$
conclusions: a pole $z'$ is inside $D$ if and only if

nodes.name: Analytic evaluation of the winding integral
nodes.statement: This integral cannot be calculated exactly using the rational Gauss-Chebyshev rules because the Chebyshev weight function is absent. However, it can be calculated analytically by breaking it up into rational-function sections, writing the integrands as rational functions, and using a partial-fraction expansion.
nodes.section: B Determining whether a pole is inside $D$

nodes.name: Fit degree-2N rational function
nodes.statement: The initial guess for the $z'_n$ is obtained by solving~\eqref{eq:Galerkin2} assuming $\widehat{W}(z) = f(z)$, which is purely real, $\widehat{Q}(z) = 1$, and then allowing $P$ and $Q$ to be of degree $2N$.
nodes.statement_short: Solve the orthogonality conditions with real data, $\widehat Q=1$, degree $2N$.

nodes.name: Pick N zeros
nodes.statement: Out of the $2N$ zeros of $Q$ we pick $N$ zeros that are outside $\Omega$, and, if there are not enough of these, we supplement them with zeros inside $\Omega$ so that we have $N$ zeros in total.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $N$ zeros, outside $\Omega$ first, supplemented by inside ones.

nodes.name: Use as initial poles
nodes.statement: These $N$ zeros are used as the poles for the first iteration.
nodes.statement_short: Return the chosen zeros as initial poles.

nodes.name: Initialize poles
nodes.statement: Set the $z'_n$ to the initial guess, as explained in Section~\ref{ssec:initial}.
nodes.statement_short: Set poles to the initial guess of Section 2.3.

nodes.name: Main loop
nodes.statement:
\WHILE {stopping criterion not met}
\STATE Solve~\eqref{eq:normalEquations} for the $a^{\mathrm{R}}_n$ and $a^{\mathrm{I}}_n$. Use only $z'_n \notin \Omega$.
\STATE Use the $a^{\mathrm{R}}_n$ and $a^{\mathrm{I}}_n$ to form $\widehat{V}$ according to~\eqref{eq:approxV} and $\widehat{W}$ according to~\eqref{eq:compPotToApprox}.
\STATE Form $\widehat{Q}$ according to~\eqref{eq:QHat}, use all $z'_n$.
\STATE Solve~\eqref{eq:Galerkin2} for $P$ and $Q$.
\STATE $z'_n = \text{roots}(Q)$.
nodes.statement_short: Iterate until the stopping criterion is met.

nodes.name: Solve for residues
nodes.statement: Solve~\eqref{eq:normalEquations} for the $a^{\mathrm{R}}_n$ and $a^{\mathrm{I}}_n$. Use only $z'_n \notin \Omega$.
nodes.statement_short: Least-squares residues using only poles outside $\Omega$.

nodes.name: Form V-hat and W-hat
nodes.statement: Use the $a^{\mathrm{R}}_n$ and $a^{\mathrm{I}}_n$ to form $\widehat{V}$ according to~\eqref{eq:approxV} and $\widehat{W}$ according to~\eqref{eq:compPotToApprox}.
nodes.statement_short: Build the conjugate estimate and boundary complex potential.

nodes.name: Form Q-hat
nodes.statement: Form $\widehat{Q}$ according to~\eqref{eq:QHat}, use all $z'_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Pole polynomial from all current poles.

nodes.name: Rational fit
nodes.statement: Solve~\eqref{eq:Galerkin2} for $P$ and $Q$.
nodes.statement_short: Solve the linearized rational fitting conditions for $P$, $Q$.

nodes.name: Relocate poles
nodes.statement: $z'_n = \text{roots}(Q)$.
nodes.statement_short: New poles are the roots of $Q$.

nodes.name: Joint least squares for residues and log coefficients
nodes.statement: Our approach is therefore to estimate the $A_j$ iteratively, along with the imaginary part of $\widetilde{W}(z)$. On each iteration, we solve \begin{equation} \begin{split} & \sum_{n = 0}^{N_\mathrm{out}} a_n^\mathrm{R} \phi_n^\mathrm{R}(z) - \sum_{n = 1}^{N_\mathrm{out}}a_n^\mathrm{I} \phi_n^\mathrm{I}(z) + \sum_{j=1}^{J}A_j \log\left|z-z^\Omega_j\right| \approx f(z), \\[1ex] & \text{with } f(z) = f_j(z) \quad \text{for } z \in \Gamma_j,\\ & \mathrm{subject \ to \ } \sum_{j=1}^{J}A_j = 0, \end{split} \end{equation} for the $a_n^\mathrm{R}$, the $a_n^\mathrm{I}$, and the $A_j$.
nodes.statement_short: Solve the constrained least squares for $a_n$ and $A_j$.

nodes.name: Eliminate A_J
nodes.statement: The condition that the sum of $A_j$'s is zero, needed to ensure the solution is bounded at infinity, can be enforced by eliminating one of the $A_j$, say, $A_{J} = - \sum_{j=1}^{J-1}A_j$. Instead of~\eqref{eq:exteriorDirichlet} we then have, \begin{equation} \sum_{n = 0}^{N_\mathrm{out}} a_n^\mathrm{R} \phi_n^\mathrm{R}(z) - \sum_{n = 1}^{N_\mathrm{out}}a_n^\mathrm{I} \phi_n^\mathrm{I}(z) + \sum_{j=1}^{J-1}A_j \log\left|\dfrac{z-z^\Omega_j}{z-z^\Omega_{J}}\right| \approx f(z). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Enforce $\sum A_j=0$ by eliminating $A_J$.

nodes.name: Solve by quadrature sampling
nodes.statement: As before, we solve~\eqref{eq:exteriorDirichlet2} by sampling at quadrature nodes, weighting the equation by the square roots of the quadrature weights, and solving the linear system in the least-squares sense. In contrast to the previous case, however, the inner products involving the logarithmic basis functions will not be integrated exactly. We must therefore add poles at infinity when deriving the quadrature rules for each section of the boundary. Fortunately, the logarithmic singularity is weak, so when the $z^\Omega_j$ are not too close to the boundary, the restriction of the logarithmic term to the boundary curve can be approximated well by piecewise polynomials. The poles at infinity added by the pole-pruning process of Section~\ref{sec:pruning} usually suffice, although extra poles at infinity can be added if necessary.
nodes.statement_short: Weighted least squares at quadrature nodes, with poles at infinity for log terms.

nodes.name: Fit rational function to W-tilde
nodes.statement: Once~\eqref{eq:exteriorDirichlet2} has been solved, a rational function is fitted to an estimate of the boundary values of $\widetilde{W}(z)$, \begin{equation} \widetilde{W}(z) \approx f(z) - \sum_{j=1}^{J-1}A_j \log\left|\dfrac{z-z^\Omega_j}{z-z^\Omega_{J}}\right| + i\widehat{V}(z), \quad z \in \bigcup_{j=1}^{J}{\Gamma_j} = \Gamma. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Run rational fitting on the log-subtracted boundary estimate of $\widetilde W$.

nodes.name: Compute logarithmic terms
nodes.statement: In this case, however, the logarithmic terms are known in advance: \begin{equation} A_j = -\dfrac{1}{2 \pi}\int_{\Gamma_j}f_j(z)|dz|, \end{equation} and they can be subtracted from the boundary data.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $A_j$ from the boundary flux.

nodes.name: Subtract logs
nodes.statement: After this subtraction, \begin{equation} \widetilde{f}_j(z) = f_j(z) - \sum_{j=1}^{J}A_j \log\left|z-z^J_j\right|, \end{equation} can be used to write a Neumann boundary condition for $\mathrm{Re}\left[\widetilde{W}(z)\right]$. Denoting $\widetilde{W}(z) = \widetilde{U}(z) + i \widetilde{V}(z)$, this condition reads, \begin{equation} \left.\dfrac{\partial \widetilde{U}}{\partial n}\right|_{\text{on }\Gamma_j} = \tilde{f}_j. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Form the log-subtracted Neumann data for $\widetilde U$.

nodes.name: Integrate to a condition on V-tilde
nodes.statement: If $\widetilde{W}(z)$ is approximated by a weighted combination of dipole potentials, it becomes inconvenient to enforce~\eqref{eq:tildeNeumann} directly, as the differentiation increases the order of the poles. Instead, we integrate~\eqref{eq:tildeNeumann} with respect to arc-length and use the Cauchy-Riemann equations to obtain, \begin{equation} \widetilde{V}(z) = \int_{z_j}^z{ \tilde{f}_j(z)|dz|} + v_j \equiv F_j(z) + v_j, \end{equation} where the integration is along $\Gamma_j$, from an arbitrary point $z_j$ to the point $z$, and the $v_j$ are constants yet to be determined.
nodes.statement_short: Integrate along arc length via Cauchy-Riemann to get $\widetilde V = F_j + v_j$.

nodes.name: Solve for residues and constants
nodes.statement: Finding a harmonic function $\widetilde{V}$ that satisfies the boundary condition~\eqref{eq:vtilde} is known as a modified Dirichlet~\cite{mikhlin1957integral} or Muskhelishvili~\cite{pogorzelski1966integral} problem, and given the condition at infinity in~\eqref{eq:neumann}, it is solvable only for a unique set of $v_j$ constants. These can be determined along with an approximate solution for $\widetilde{V}$, by solving \begin{equation} \sum_{n = 1}^{N_\mathrm{out}} a_n^\mathrm{R} \phi_n^\mathrm{I}(z) + a_n^\mathrm{I} \phi_n^\mathrm{R}(z) - v_j \approx F_j(z), \quad \text{for} \ z \in \Gamma_j, \end{equation} for the $a^\mathrm{R}_n$, the $a^\mathrm{I}_n$, and the $v_j$.
nodes.statement_short: Least squares for residues and the unknown constants $v_j$.

nodes.name: Apply rational fitting
nodes.statement: As before,~\eqref{eq:neumannResidues} is solved in the least-squares sense after sampling the basis functions at quadrature nodes and weighting the equations by the square roots of quadrature weights. Once~\eqref{eq:neumannResidues} is solved, the rational fitting algorithm is applied to an estimate of the boundary values of $\widetilde{W}(z)$ given by, \begin{equation} \widetilde{W}(z) \approx \sum_{n = 1}^{N_\mathrm{out}} a_n^\mathrm{I} \phi_n^\mathrm{I}(z) + a_n^\mathrm{R} \phi_n^\mathrm{R}(z) + i \left[ F_j(z) + v_j\right], \quad \text{for} \ z \in \Gamma_j. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Quadrature least squares, then rational fitting on the estimate of $\widetilde W$.

nodes.name: Partition into clusters
nodes.statement: The scheme consists of partitioning the boundary curves into clusters so that each curve belongs to a single cluster, as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:clust}.
nodes.statement_short: Partition curves into clusters.

nodes.name: k-means on centroids
nodes.statement: Various algorithms for obtaining such a partition exist, and we use the simplest one, the $k$-means clustering, or Lloyd's, algorithm~\cite{lloyd1982least}. To keep the partitioning simple, each curve is entirely within one cluster and represented by its centroid, on which the clustering algorithm operates.
nodes.statement_short: Cluster curve centroids with Lloyd's $k$-means.

nodes.name: Add buffer regions
nodes.statement: Then, to each cluster we add a ``buffer region,'' as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:clust}, so that curves close to the edge of the cluster have all their nearby interactions taken into account. The buffer region is obtained by adding to each curve all the curves with centroids closer than some radius, and this radius is chosen as twice the distance to the nearest centroid among all other curves.
nodes.statement_short: Add neighbouring curves within twice the nearest-centroid distance.

nodes.name: Discard buffer poles
nodes.statement: Poles that, after the local optimization, are found inside the buffer region are not used when solving the full problem.
nodes.statement_short: Drop poles lying in buffer regions for the full solve.

nodes.name: Discretize the rational fitting problem
nodes.statement: Using the quadrature rules of Section~\ref{ssec:quadForIRF}, we discretize the continuous norm in~\eqref{eq:minProbIRF} and write the minimization problem as, \begin{equation} \min_{\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}} \, \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{n=0}^N{ \dfrac{\sqrt{\lambda_k}}{\widehat{Q}(z_k)}\left|{b_n z_k^n - a_n z_k^n \widehat{W}(z_k) }\right|} \end{equation} in which the unknowns are the monomial coefficients of $P(z)$ and $Q(z)$, denoted $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{a}$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Discretize the weighted norm at quadrature nodes in monomial coefficients.

nodes.name: Rewrite in matrix form
nodes.statement:
Let us rewrite~\eqref{eq:minProb} in matrix form, using the notation  egin{align} \mathbf{\Lambda} &= 	ext{diag}(\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots, \lambda_K),
otag \ \mathbf{\widehat{Q}} &= 	ext{diag}\left[\widehat{Q}(z_1), \widehat{Q}(z_2), \ldots, \widehat{Q}(z_K)ight],
otag \ \mathbf{\widehat{W}} &= 	ext{diag}\left[\widehat{W}(z_1), \widehat{W}(z_2), \ldots, \widehat{W}(z_K)ight],\ V_{kn} &= z_k^n, \quad n=0,1,\ldots,N,
otag \ \mathbf{c} &=  egin{bmatrix} \mathbf{b}\ \mathbf{a}\ \end{bmatrix}.
otag \end{align} We obtain,  egin{equation} \min_{\mathbf{c}} \, \left|\left|\mathbf{\Lambda}^ rac{1}{2} \mathbf{\widehat{Q}}^{-1}\left[\mathbf{V}, -\mathbf{\widehat{W}}\mathbf{V}ight]\mathbf{c}ight|ight|. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Matrix least squares with Vandermonde blocks.

nodes.name: Arnoldi orthonormal bases
nodes.statement: To deal with this problem, we construct two orthonormal bases, one for the column space of $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{\Lambda}^\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{\widehat{Q}}^{-1}\mathbf{V}$ and one for the column space of $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{\Lambda}^\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{\widehat{Q}}^{-1}\mathbf{\widehat{W}V}$. This can be done with the Arnoldi iteration~\cite{arnoldi1951principle,saad2003iterative}, by noting that the columns of $\mathbf{A}$ form a Krylov subspace, \begin{equation} K= \text{span}[\mathbf{d}, \mathbf{Z}\mathbf{d}, \mathbf{Z}^2\mathbf{d}, \ldots, \mathbf{Z}^N\mathbf{d}], \end{equation} where $\mathbf{Z} = \mathrm{diag}\left(z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_K\right)$ and $\mathbf{d} = \mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{\Lambda}^\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{\widehat{Q}}^{-1})$, and similarly for the columns of $\mathbf{B}$.
nodes.statement_short: Build orthonormal bases of colsp(A) and colsp(B) by Arnoldi on a Krylov subspace.

nodes.name: Change basis and normalize
nodes.statement: Once we have constructed the orthonormal bases, \begin{align} \mathrm{colsp}(\mathbf{P}) &= \mathrm{colsp}(\mathbf{A}), \quad \mathbf{P^\dagger P} = \mathbf{I} \\ \mathrm{colsp}(\mathbf{Q}) &= \mathrm{colsp}(\mathbf{B}), \quad \mathbf{Q^\dagger Q} = \mathbf{I}, \end{align} we rewrite~\eqref{eq:irfDiscrete} in the new basis, \begin{equation} \min_{\mathbf{\tilde{c}}} \, \left|\left|\left[\mathbf{P}, -\mathbf{Q}\right]\mathbf{\tilde{c}}\right|\right|, \end{equation} and impose the normalization condition $\tilde{c}_{2N} = 1$, which corresponds to $Q(z)$ being monic in the new basis.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the problem in the orthonormal bases with $Q$ monic.

nodes.name: Solve least squares
nodes.statement: The solution of the minimization problem is then obtained by solving the over-determined linear system \begin{equation} [\mathbf{P},-\mathbf{Q}_{1:N-1}]\mathbf{\tilde{c}} = \mathbf{Q}_N \end{equation} in the least-squares sense.
nodes.statement_short: Solve the overdetermined system for $\tilde{\mathbf c}$.

nodes.name: Poles from companion matrix
nodes.statement: Once~\eqref{eq:irfDiscrete} is solved, the zeros of $Q(z)$, which are the poles for the next iteration, can be obtained without transforming back to the monomial basis. They are the eigenvalues of a generalized companion matrix~\cite{coelho1999robust}, \begin{equation} \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{H}_{1:N,1:N} - H_{N+1,N}\,\mathbf{\tilde{c}}_{N+1:2N}\,\mathbf{e}_N^T, \end{equation} where $\mathbf{e}_N$ is the $N^\text{th}$ column of the order-$N$ identity matrix and $\mathbf{H}$ is the upper Hessenberg matrix obtained from the Arnoldi iteration used to generate the orthonormal basis for colsp($\mathbf{B}$).
nodes.statement_short: New poles are eigenvalues of a generalized companion matrix.
